newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: China says expects WTO talks concluded in 1997.
newsitem.headline: China says expects WTO talks concluded in 1997.

text.p: China expects to conclude its talks with the United States over its accession to the World Trade Organisation in the first half of next year, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said on Monday.

The talks were likely to be completed before U.S. President Bill Clinton and China's President Jiang Zemin exchanged the state visits announced after they met in Manila on Sunday, Qian told a news conference.
Qian was speaking after Clinton and Jiang attended the one-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit at Subic Bay north of Manila on Monday.
News of the exchange of visits, a major thaw between the two powers after nearly a decade of frost, was one of the main highlights of the summit and the meetings that preceded it.
Asked when he expected the talks with the United States to be concluded, Qian replied: "You can consider it to be in the first half of next year or before the exchange of state visits."
But he made it clear this was not a condition for the state visits taking place.
"There's no direct link between the date of the visits of heads of state and the date of China's entry into the WTO," he said, speaking through an interpreter.
Washington's insistence that China join as a developed member rather than on the easier terms available to under-developed nations is one of the main obstacles to China's membership in the WTO.

Qian said China was generally pleased with the outcome of the APEC summit and the Manila Action Plan it produced which is designed to map out how the 18-member grouping will reach its goal of setting up the world's biggest free trade region by 2020.
"This will have a positive impact on the future development of APEC," Qian said.
During the summit, President Jiang had stressed the importance of economic and technical cooperation to APEC's development, Qian said.
The grouping had concentrated for too long on fostering trade and investment liberalisation, Qian quote Jiang as saying.
The Manila Action Plan provides details of how the region's developed nations should assist their less well-off partners through the exchange of technical and economic expertise.
Qian said China also planned to broaden the range of products on which it would lower tariffs.
In its own individual action plan for APEC, China has said it will lower its average tariff rate to 15 percent from the current 23 percent by 2000.
Other nations, however, have said that previous reductions in China's tariffs have been limited to a relatively small range of goods, mainly raw materials instead of manufactured products.
